name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Thursday 17 May 1973

clue.text: Capital is what hands need not return

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the word is read from its end to its start

blocks.note: dirty hands need a wash; read as the noun for that cleaning
taken as written, then turned round

explanation.surface: A remark that dirty hands need never come back for more cleaning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'need not' reads as a single phrase meaning 'do not have to', but 'need' ends the first piece and 'not' starts the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Washington DC is the seat of government of the United States, its national capital city.

clue.text: Eugene's article is writ ten up in Ethiopia

definitions.note: the clue gives the place, the answer names a city there

indicators.note: in a down entry, written up means set down from bottom to top, so the letters climb backwards

blocks.note: Eugene Aram was an 18th-century English murderer made famous by a Bulwer-Lytton novel
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Some man named Eugene owns an article that has been written up, oddly split as 'writ ten'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'writ ten' is just 'written' broken into two words to disguise the reversal signal. In 1973 Eritrea was part of Ethiopia.
explanation.definitionFit: Asmara was then a city of the Ethiopian empire, capital of its Eritrean province, so it is a place found there.

clue.text: Oxford college alters the right of way

indicators.note: to alter is to change, so the following letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the standard abbreviation for right
a ford is a way across a river

explanation.surface: An Oxford college changes the public right of way across its grounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right of way' reads as a single legal phrase, but 'right' and 'way' do separate jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Hertford College is one of the constituent colleges of the University of Oxford.

clue.text: Fruit drink in Middle West

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central portion, so only those inner letters are kept

blocks.note: nectar is a sweet drink, the drink of the gods
taken as written
the two central letters of the word

explanation.surface: A fruit drink served somewhere in the American Middle West.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Middle West' looks like the region; here 'Middle' just picks the centre of 'West'.
explanation.definitionFit: A nectarine is a smooth-skinned variety of peach, a stone fruit.

clue.text: Number on bale is wrong, it might be maintained

indicators.note: something wrong is out of order, so these letters need rearranging

blocks.note: ten is a number
the letters of this word rearranged

explanation.surface: The number stamped on a bale is wrong, though someone might still defend it.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, 'on' puts the number above the second piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenable position or argument is one that can be defended or held, that is, upheld against attack.

clue.text: Get this animal in one attempt?

indicators.note: 'in' says the wanted word sits inside the following words, running across them

blocks.note: the letters straddle the break between the two words

explanation.surface: A hunter hopes to bag a beast at the very first try.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a whole-clue riddle, but the answer lies in plain sight across 'one attempt'.
explanation.definitionFit: Neat is an archaic or dialect word for a bovine animal, an ox or cow, as in neatsfoot oil.

clue.text: Good heavens! Is that on TV?

blocks.note: surface reading: an exclamation of surprise at something seen on television
setter's reading: the heavens taken literally as the abode of the blessed, with the question teasing whether such bliss could be broadcast

explanation.walkthrough: 'Good heavens!' is read literally as the blissful heavens rather than as an oath; the question just keeps the viewer's surprised tone.
explanation.definitionFit: Paradise is heaven, the blissful home of the righteous after death.

clue.text: Defenders in a game — the real point's the second half

blocks.note: taken as written
polo is a game played on horseback
the gist is the real point, with its 's kept as S

explanation.surface: In some game the defenders are the key, and the second half decides it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the second half' just says the point comes after the game in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Apologists are people who argue in defence of a belief, cause or person.

clue.text: Settle with the gypsies? (Strike afterwards)

blocks.note: surface reading: going to live among travelling people
setter's reading: setting up tents for the night, as travellers do, then striking camp, taking the tents down, the next morning

explanation.walkthrough: The parenthesis is the hint: you strike a camp you have set up, so settling here is pitching tents for a while.
explanation.definitionFit: To encamp is to settle in a temporary camp of tents, as travellers or an army do.

clue.text: A man gets around little by little, like 1 ac

indicators.note: to get around something is to surround it, so one word goes inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
'Eric, or Little by Little' is an 1858 Victorian school story by Dean Farrar

explanation.surface: A man travels about slowly, bit by bit, like some cross-reference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little by little' looks like an adverb but stands for the novel's title character. 1 across is WASHINGTON.
explanation.definitionFit: Washington, the capital of the United States, is American, so something like it shares that nationality.

clue.text: Last, in spite of everything

blocks.note: first meaning: coming after every other one
second meaning: the everyday phrase for nevertheless

explanation.walkthrough: Taken literally the phrase means following everybody, which is to come last.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase literally describes what follows every other item, and idiomatically means nevertheless or regardless.

clue.text: Irish county clinic

blocks.note: first meaning: a county in the west of Ireland
second meaning: the famous American medical centre in Rochester, Minnesota

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a clinic located in an Irish county; the two are unrelated uses of one name.
explanation.definitionFit: Mayo is a county of Connacht, and the Mayo Clinic is a renowned US hospital.

clue.text: Religious person acted badly, put in complaint

indicators.note: something put in another thing sits inside it, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: a moan is a complaint
to ham is to overact, to perform badly

explanation.surface: A devout person behaved badly and then grumbled about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The older term, now considered dated or offensive, for a follower of Islam.
explanation.definitionFit: An outdated name for a Muslim, a follower of the faith taught by the Prophet, hence a religious person.

clue.text: Demoting a team, for example, and telling about it

indicators.note: about means around, so the telling surrounds the example placed within

blocks.note: relating a story is telling it
e.g. abbreviates exempli gratia, for example

explanation.surface: A club is sent down a division and someone recounts the story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' points back to 'for example', which goes inside the telling.
explanation.definitionFit: Relegation in football leagues is the demotion of a team to a lower division at season's end.

clue.text: Signal to go given by admiral to the Mayfly

blocks.note: a green light means go
Sir Francis Drake, the Elizabethan admiral

explanation.surface: An admiral hoists a signal giving a ship named Mayfly permission to sail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Mayfly' reads like a ship's name, but it is the insect.
explanation.definitionFit: Green drake is an anglers' name for the common mayfly, especially its subimago stage used in fly fishing.

clue.text: The Warden of the White House

blocks.note: first meaning: Septimus, the title character of Trollope's novel The Warden
second meaning: Warren G., US president in the early 1920s

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a guard at the president's residence; instead it is one surname shared by a Victorian fictional cleric and an American president.
explanation.definitionFit: Septimus Harding is Trollope's warden of Hiram's Hospital, and Warren Harding occupied the presidential residence 1921-23.

clue.text: Disparages NUR's arrangement with county

indicators.note: an arrangement puts things in a new order, so these letters are reordered

blocks.note: the NUR was Britain's National Union of Railwaymen; its letters with the S
County Down is in Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: The railway union belittles a deal struck with a county council.
explanation.walkthrough: The NUR was Britain's National Union of Railwaymen.
explanation.definitionFit: To run someone down is the idiom for criticising them unfairly or belittling them.

clue.text: But green ones may be experienced of course

definitions.text: But green ones may be experienced of course

blocks.clueFragment: But green ones may be experienced
blocks.note: surface reading: a paradox that green, meaning novice, people can be experienced
setter's reading: on a golf course, the staff who tend the greens may well be veterans

explanation.walkthrough: 'green' reads as inexperienced; it is the putting green, and 'of course' means belonging to a golf course rather than naturally.
explanation.definitionFit: Greenkeepers maintain golf greens, so the answer is the people who look after something.

clue.text: PC takes in a single striker — he's not militant

indicators.note: to take in is to admit inside, so the first piece wraps round the next

blocks.note: PC, police constable, taken as written
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one
a fist is what strikes a blow

explanation.surface: A police constable arrests a lone picket on strike who turns out to be peaceful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'striker' suggests an industrial dispute or footballer, but it is just the thing you hit with.
explanation.definitionFit: A pacifist opposes war and violence, so he is the opposite of militant.

clue.text: Fish a fiancee shows to friends

blocks.note: a fiancee is a woman, referred to as her
what a newly engaged woman shows off: her engagement band

explanation.surface: A newly engaged woman proudly displays something to her friends.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is read as a phrase: what she shows is her ring.
explanation.definitionFit: The herring is a common silvery food fish of the North Atlantic.

clue.text: Some gannet built in this tree

indicators.note: something built is put together from parts, so these letters are assembled anew

blocks.note: both words used letter for letter

explanation.surface: A seabird has made its nest up in a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' looks like a vague quantity, but its letters are part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The mangosteen is a tropical evergreen tree of South-East Asia, bearing a prized purple fruit.

clue.text: Whence corn for horses?

blocks.note: first meaning: the cores on which maize kernels grow
second meaning: sturdy short-legged riding horses

explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks where horse feed comes from; the answer word means both the corn's source and the horses.
explanation.definitionFit: Maize kernels grow on a cob, the place they come from, and a cob is also a stocky breed of horse.

clue.text: Rob poor soldier of horse

indicators.note: poor means in bad shape, so the word is knocked out of order

blocks.note: taken as written, letters to rearrange
a non-commissioned officer, such as a sergeant

explanation.surface: A thief steals a horse from a poor soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rob' looks like the verb steal; it is just three letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A bronco is a wild or half-tamed horse of the western United States.

clue.text: Tip the test questions found in book, perhaps

blocks.note: the tip of something is its end
an exam paper is a set of test questions

explanation.surface: A tip-off reveals the exam questions hidden in a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Endpapers are the blank leaves pasted inside the front and back covers of a bound volume.

clue.text: Used to call for Tom?

blocks.note: surface reading: a word once used when calling for a man named Tom
setter's reading: a tom is a male cat, and people call a cat with this word

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tom' looks like a person; it is a tomcat, summoned with the usual pet name for a cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Puss is the familiar name used when calling or addressing a cat.

clue.text: Native return for a French delicacy at one

definitions.note: singular in the clue; the answer is plural

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the whole string is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: snails, escargots, are a French delicacy
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A local sends back a French delicacy at one restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: the answer is natives of a country, and the clue's 'Native' must be read as a collective.
explanation.definitionFit: Italians are the people born in Italy, its natives.

clue.text: Invariably, say law breakers

indicators.note: breakers smash things apart, so these letters are broken up and remade

blocks.note: both words used letter for letter

explanation.surface: People who break the law always do so, some say.
explanation.definitionFit: Always means at all times without exception, which is what invariably means too.

clue.text: No, it's to urge on the country to back the proposal

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so all these letters run from right to left

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, apostrophe dropped
to egg someone on is to urge them
the US, the United States

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to push the nation into supporting a proposal.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole run of pieces from 'No' to 'the country' is reversed together.
explanation.definitionFit: A suggestion is an idea put forward for consideration, which is what a proposal is.
